beats.trigger: Security
beats.got: nothing new, just a header

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe by looking at its output.
beats.got: output alone doesn't prove safety, so you need a separate check. fair, though I'd have guessed that

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent, (2) agent risk layered on top of normal security work.
beats.got: nothing new, a reading list

beats.trigger: residual risk: what's left after mitigation, and what future sessions need before they touch the system
beats.got: the day is about writing down what's left over after a fix. I've never done that formally

beats.trigger: You've had three agents search your company and three more decide.
beats.got: the deciders trust whatever the searchers bring back and nobody checks in between. I'd never framed my own setups that way

beats.trigger: It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: nothing new, I use tool calls daily. I ran the three prompts without reading the answers

beats.trigger: Agent systems don't hand you certainty.
beats.got: nothing new, you don't get certainty so you run a loop

beats.trigger: The story works because classical software is deterministic (same input, same output).
beats.got: nothing new. deterministic software vs agents is old news for my engineers

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: the attack is plain english inside a doc the agent reads, so the perimeter can't see it. I knew injection existed but not framed as persuasion

beats.trigger: Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels).
beats.got: five mitigations built for agents: scope, split, filter, gate, review. split by trust level is the useful one for org-wide rollouts

beats.trigger: Closing one takes evidence, not a better guess.
beats.got: after a fix you write down what's left, then accept it or close the door. a bit like ceremony until I see it in a real report

beats.trigger: Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: every agent I've built got more access over time. cutting access shrinks the damage when it's wrong. that's the opposite of what I do on weekends

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature somebody in your company wanted.
beats.got: don't connect it in the first place is the cheapest fix. a vendor admitting that a smaller agent is a smaller sale is rare

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new, a recap: run the loop, name the residual, decide

beats.trigger: Module 4 is the canonical place this authoring lands.
beats.got: nothing new. I already write skills, this is the intro for people who don't

beats.trigger: CLASS-1 call: the policy contradicts itself on missing labels.
beats.got: the agent audited my files against the policies and found a contradiction inside the policy itself. 18 rules, 9 'can't tell'. more honest than I expected

beats.trigger: CLAUDE.md also says the agent "may send".
beats.got: my own rule 'nothing gets sent without me' contradicts my own agent file. the agent caught it because I stated the rule first. that stung a bit

beats.trigger: I wrote this skill in-session and no human has reviewed it.
beats.got: the agent flagged that its own skill is unreviewed and that three rule IDs I'd named don't exist. it refused to guess instead of making up a mapping

beats.trigger: Push back until the report shape is narrow enough that you will actually read it on Monday.
beats.got: keep the report short enough that someone reads it. I answered the grill in one go and let it choose the rest

beats.trigger: Session skill lists usually load at session start, so you may need a new session before it appears.
beats.got: copy the folder into .claude/skills and restart. the clash with the built-in security-audit skill was the only interesting bit

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: nothing new, you now have a packaged check you can rerun

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: the point is running the loop once on my own system, not getting a pass

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: nothing new, check the skill loaded

beats.trigger: N-2: The injection was removed and logged at memory/index.md:15, but its author is still unknown.
beats.got: a real prompt injection was already sitting in the data the memo agent reads. someone planted it in OneDrive and nobody knows who. the packaged run also corrected a wrong 'compliant' from the raw run

beats.trigger: Combined with the send gate, a repeat would reach the CEO unread.
beats.got: an agent that can send to the CEO without review plus an injection that's already happened once is a real incident path. I'd have shipped that and called it good

beats.trigger: The new rule is prose: the agent can still read the raw original and the archive, write anywhere, and its send permission is unchanged.
beats.got: the fix was a paragraph in a markdown file, so it's only as strong as the agent's compliance. real enforcement means removing the tool permission, not adding a sentence

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can actually answer is sitting in the report.
beats.got: bring the report and a narrow question to legal or security, not the whole mess. I'm the CTO, so mostly I am that person

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent.
beats.got: most of what my team runs is prototype by this definition. short and fair

beats.trigger: The unease that remains is what the loop is supposed to produce, not what it failed to remove.
beats.got: nothing new, a recap: two reports, one fix, one residual

beats.trigger: The next agent you build will have a stricter starting line because of this one.
beats.got: the audit findings get written into the root CLAUDE.md as standing rules, so the next session starts with them. that compounding is useful for a whole org

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: a skill is the simplest way to hand a method to non-engineers. it doesn't solve who owns or maintains it, and that's my exact blocker

beats.trigger: Well-formed English is the attack surface, direct or through a source the agent reads.
beats.got: nothing new, four bullet recap

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors.
beats.got: homework: one sentence per case. I'd probably skip it and catch up live

beats.trigger: Carry the risk discipline from this module into both cases: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: two real cases, a lawyer filing fake citations and a consultancy report with made-up content, where nobody checked the agent's output. that's my 'checking is for beginners' belief with names on it

take_homes: an agent can audit its own setup and find what I'd have skipped: a planted injection already in the data and a memo agent that could send to the CEO unreviewed. checking output isn't beginner stuff
give it less: scope or remove the tool before writing rules. a rule in a markdown file is weak compared with taking away the permission
a packaged two-lens audit skill plus operating rules in the root instructions file is a reusable way to start the next agent stricter, and to hand to others

monday.move: run the security-audit skill on the agents my engineers have wired to send, write or post, and check the send and write permissions first
monday.stop_condition: a ranked list of agents with send or write reach outside their job, each with an owner and a keep or cut call
monday.blocker: no company policy files, since the module used a reference set; and no one owns agent definitions across teams. the org-wide sales build waits until the send gate question is answered

misconception.why: the memo agent was good and still had an injection already hit it, plus a send path to the CEO with no review; the raw run also got a row wrong that the packaged one caught. I still think reviewing every output is overkill, but unchecked send paths are not fine

one_line: first hour is stuff my engineers already know, but the part where the agent audits your own setup and finds an injection already sitting in your data is worth the day; skip the homework
